newsitem.title: FRANCE: No EU decision yet on wheat export bids.
newsitem.headline: No EU decision yet on wheat export bids.

text.p: The European Commission has yet to decide whether to accept bids for more than 700,000 tonnes of wheat export licences, European grain sources said on Monday.

The bids, for licences valid until the end of December at a fixed tax of 0.50 Ecus, were posted via France last Friday. The Commission has until Wednesday to use its three-day veto if it wants to halt the automatic process of accepting them.
"There is no decision and the Commission has until Tuesday evening to decide but there is no drama," a grain source said.
The European Commission had no official comment.

Bidding for the licences soared on the first day of August and just one day after the EU pegged its daily export value for soft wheat at a standing tax of 0.50 Ecus per tonne. Wheat had previously been tagged with no value -- tax or subsidy -- meaning it could be exported at domestic prices with some risk.
Traders said the dollar's rampage and a bullish tone in world wheat had sparked the rush for licences, which on current values made Europe competitive for far-off delivery positions.

Another piece of bait had been the chance to secure an extra month -- December -- in the validity of licences granted now, compared to those granted in July. EU export licences are valid for the month in which they are issued plus another four months.
Whether the EU is willing to release the wheat and encourage further bids depends in part on the reason behind its original decision not to penalise the daily mechanism, traders said.

The Commission -- which usually offers its best refunds or lowest taxes through the more rigid weekly tender -- put a fixed tax of 0.5 Ecus on its first-come-first-served daily channel for licences on Thursday, identical to the lowest tax at the tender.

Traders saw the move then as a way of smoothing short-term exports for operators who were still short of licences -- at some cost but at reasonably comfortable levels -- during a two-week holiday gap in the main tender system until August 14.

But shifting wheat and currency values increasingly make the same licences worth having for those building up long positions in EU wheat later this year. Traders have been given few clues on how far the Commission is prepared to go along with this.
Traders peg French wheat about $2 a tonne over U.S. soft red for August but $2 under for December based on a 0.5 Ecu tax.
A senior European grain source declined to say why the daily channel had been left open at the current level and what volume of awards the Commission would tolerate over coming weeks.

But while not ruling out some intervention, he pointed out several factors giving the EU extra leeway this year. Internal prices were "not excessively high," the EU was heading for a big crop and the dollar and world market were doing well, he said.
"That does not mean that (the Commission) does not have to manage the situation," he added.
For the past two years the Commission has explicitly tied exports to the control of internal prices at the insistence of EU farm ministers. But internal prices now are relatively flat.
If the Commission did decide to cool exports, its options would include rejecting Friday's wheat bids, rejecting any further ones, raising the daily tax or a combination of these.
